Sustained energy failure and activation of apoptotic and stress programmes in the fiber proceed to frank fiber breakdown when exposure is high enough or prolonged enough.

Muscle pain arises at this sub-necrotic level of injury rather than from fiber breakdown: the stratum in which myalgia is commonest is defined by a normal creatine kinase, so muscle pain is reported where fibers are not breaking down. What converts myocyte stress into the sensation of pain is not established, which is why the intermediates are recorded as unknown.
Creatine kinase enters the circulation from broken-down fibers.
Loss of functioning fibers produces objective weakness. Note that the subjective weakness reported in SAMS, where creatine kinase is normal, is not this edge: it arises upstream of necrosis.
Fiber breakdown is what a pathologist observes on biopsy as necrotic fibers, which is how this mechanism becomes an examinable finding.
Extensive fiber breakdown with biochemical evidence of end-organ damage is what the trial literature defines as rhabdomyolysis.
Myoglobin held in the fiber enters the bloodstream when the fiber breaks down.
Filtered myoglobin appears in the urine, which is the clinically visible sign of this burden.
Myoglobin deposited in the tubule is directly toxic to tubular epithelium.

Increased availability of the autoantigen is the proposed route by which an antibody response against it arises in a susceptible person. The intermediates are unknown: antigen induction is shown in cultured cells, and what carries it from there to a human autoantibody response is not established.

The antibody response is accompanied by necrotizing muscle injury that responds to immunosuppression rather than to drug withdrawal, which is the basis for treating it as immune-mediated. The intermediates are recorded as unknown because what the antibody does to the fiber is exactly what is unsettled: the candidate effector was terminal complement, and the one trial that inhibited it in patients was negative.
The autoimmune route converges on the same fiber breakdown as the direct toxic route, which is why both produce creatine kinase release and proximal weakness.
Pharyngeal muscle involvement in more severe disease.
Sustained impairment of glucose handling is what is diagnosed as new-onset diabetes when it crosses the diagnostic threshold.

Hepatocyte injury releases aminotransferases. The intermediates are recorded as unknown because the mitochondrial lesion is demonstrated in vitro while the clinical enzyme elevation is observed separately, and the two have not been joined in patients.
Taking the drug is what establishes the systemic exposure the rest of the pathograph follows from. Dose determines how much.

nodes.description: Reduced-function variants of two transporters that between them govern how much of an administered dose reaches the systemic circulation. OATP1B1, encoded by SLCO1B1, is the hepatic uptake transporter, so reduced function lowers hepatic extraction of the drug. BCRP, encoded by ABCG2, is an efflux transporter whose contribution to statin disposition is not hepatic extraction, so reduced function is recorded here as raising systemic availability without this entry asserting which compartment it acts in - the source measures accumulation, not its site. This node is host susceptibility rather than drug action: it injures nothing by itself, and its only consequence in this pathograph is the concentration reached by a given dose. It is absent in most people who develop toxicity, so the chain below it runs with or without it.
